koko-eating-bananas.pattern: Binary search on the answer (smallest speed for which a monotone check passes)

approaches.name: Try every speed from 1 upwards
approaches.idea: At speed `k`, pile `p` takes `ceil(p / k)` hours. Try k = 1, 2, 3, … and return the first speed whose total hours fit in `h`.
steps: For `k = 1, 2, …` up to the largest pile:
Add up `ceil(p / k)` over all piles (as a 64-bit number).
Return the first `k` whose total is at most `h` (the largest pile always works, since then every pile takes 1 hour and `h >= piles.length`).
approaches.why: M is the largest pile (up to 10⁹); each speed costs a pass over the n piles.

approaches.name: Binary search the speed
approaches.idea: A faster speed never needs more hours, so "can finish within h" is false for small speeds and true from some speed on. Binary search for the first speed where it is true.
steps: Search `k` in `[1, max(piles)]`.
`mid` is feasible if `sum(ceil(p / mid)) <= h`.
If feasible, the answer is `mid` or smaller: `hi = mid`; otherwise `lo = mid + 1`.
Return `lo`.
approaches.why: About log₂(10⁹) ≈ 30 checks, each a pass over n piles. `ceil(p / k)` is computed as `(p + k − 1) / k` in integers; the hour total needs 64 bits.

find-the-smallest-divisor-given-a-thresh.pattern: Binary search on the answer (the rounded-up sum only shrinks as the divisor grows)

approaches.name: Try every divisor from 1 upwards
approaches.idea: Compute the rounded-up sum for d = 1, 2, 3, … and return the first d whose sum is within the threshold.
steps: For `d = 1, 2, …`: compute `sum(ceil(x / d))`.
Return the first `d` with sum `<= threshold`.
It stops by `d = max(nums)` at the latest, where every term is 1 and the sum is `n <= threshold`.
approaches.why: M = max(nums) candidates (up to 10⁶), each costing a pass over n values.

approaches.name: Binary search the divisor
approaches.idea: A larger divisor never increases the rounded-up sum, so "sum ≤ threshold" flips from false to true exactly once. Binary search for that point.
steps: Search `d` in `[1, max(nums)]`.
If `sum(ceil(x / mid)) <= threshold`, set `hi = mid`; else `lo = mid + 1`.
Return `lo`.
approaches.why: About 20 checks for M = 10⁶, each O(n).

capacity-to-ship-packages-within-d-days.pattern: Binary search on the answer with a greedy feasibility check

approaches.name: Try every capacity from the heaviest package up
approaches.idea: The capacity must be at least the heaviest package. Try each capacity from there and simulate loading greedily; the first that ships in time is the answer.
steps: For `cap` from `max(weights)` up to `sum(weights)`:
Simulate: fill the current day until the next package would exceed `cap`, then start a new day; count the days.
Return the first `cap` needing at most `days` days.
approaches.why: Up to S = sum(weights) capacities (about 2.5 × 10⁷ here), each simulated in O(n).

approaches.name: Binary search the capacity
approaches.idea: More capacity never needs more days, so the check flips once. Search between the heaviest package (smallest possible) and the total weight (ships everything in one day).
steps: Set `lo = max(weights)`, `hi = sum(weights)`.
For `mid`, count the days the greedy loading needs.
If that is `<= days`, set `hi = mid`; otherwise `lo = mid + 1`.
Return `lo`.
approaches.why: About log₂(S) ≈ 25 simulations of O(n) each. Greedy loading is optimal for a fixed capacity: sailing later can never help, since order is fixed.

minimum-number-of-days-to-make-m-bouquet.pattern: Binary search on the day with a greedy count of adjacent bloomed runs

approaches.name: Try each bloom day as the answer, earliest first
approaches.idea: The answer is always one of the bloom days (nothing new blooms between them). Sort the distinct bloom days and test each in turn by counting bouquets.
steps: If `m × k > n`, return −1: there are not enough flowers (compute in 64 bits).
Sort the distinct values of `bloomDay`.
For each day `d` in increasing order, walk the flowers counting runs of bloomed (`<= d`) flowers; every `k` in a row make a bouquet.
Return the first `d` that gives at least `m` bouquets.
approaches.why: Up to n distinct days, each checked in O(n), after an O(n log n) sort. The sorted list of days takes O(n).

approaches.name: Binary search the day
approaches.idea: Waiting longer never gives fewer bouquets, so "at least m bouquets by day d" flips from false to true once. Binary search the day between the earliest and latest bloom.
steps: If `m × k > n`, return −1 (64-bit multiply).
Search `d` in `[min(bloomDay), max(bloomDay)]`.
Count bouquets on day `mid` greedily (runs of `k` bloomed neighbours). If at least `m`, set `hi = mid`; else `lo = mid + 1`.
Return `lo`.
approaches.why: D is the range of bloom days (up to 10⁹), so about 30 passes of O(n). Taking a bouquet as soon as a run reaches k is optimal: using the leftmost flowers never blocks a later bouquet.

minimum-time-to-complete-trips.pattern: Binary search on time (trips completed by time t = Σ ⌊t / time[i]⌋ only grows)

approaches.name: Advance the clock one unit at a time
approaches.idea: By time `t`, bus `i` has finished `t / time[i]` trips (rounded down). Increase `t` from 1 until the total reaches `totalTrips`.
steps: Add up `t / time[i]` over all buses, stopping early once it reaches `totalTrips`.
Return the first `t` whose total is at least `totalTrips`.
approaches.why: T is the answer itself, which can reach 10¹⁴ (one slow bus making 10⁷ trips).

approaches.name: Binary search the time
approaches.idea: More time never means fewer trips, so binary search the first `t` with enough trips. The fastest bus alone finishes `totalTrips` trips by `min(time) × totalTrips`, which bounds the search.
steps: Set `lo = 1`, `hi = min(time) × totalTrips` (64-bit).
For `mid`, add up `mid / time[i]`, stopping once it reaches `totalTrips` (this also prevents overflow).
If enough, `hi = mid`; else `lo = mid + 1`.
Return `lo`.
approaches.why: T ≤ 10¹⁴, so about 47 checks, each O(n). Stopping the sum early keeps it below 2·10⁷ + 10¹⁴, far from overflow.

magnetic-force-between-two-balls.pattern: Binary search on the answer (largest gap for which greedy placement fits m balls)

approaches.name: Try every distance from the largest possible down
approaches.idea: After sorting, a minimum gap `d` is possible if placing balls greedily (first basket, then the next basket at least `d` further) fits `m` balls. The gap can be at most `(last − first) / (m − 1)`; try every value from there downwards.
steps: Sort the positions.
For `d` from `(pos[n − 1] − pos[0]) / (m − 1)` down to 1:
Place greedily and count the balls; return the first `d` that fits `m` balls.
approaches.why: R = (largest − smallest) / (m − 1) candidates, each checked in O(n), plus the sort. When the answer is far below R this is far too slow.

approaches.name: Binary search the largest feasible gap
approaches.idea: If gap `d` is achievable, every smaller gap is too. So "fits m balls" is true up to some `d` and false after: binary search the last true value.
steps: Sort the positions. Search `d` in `[1, (pos[n − 1] − pos[0]) / (m − 1)]`.
Use the upper middle `mid = lo + (hi − lo + 1) / 2`; check by greedy placement.
If it fits, `lo = mid`; else `hi = mid − 1`.
Return `lo`.
approaches.time: O(n log n + n log R)
approaches.why: Sorting costs O(n log n) (plus its own stack); then about 30 greedy checks of O(n). Greedy placement is optimal for a fixed gap: putting each ball as far left as allowed leaves the most room for the rest.

split-array-largest-sum.pattern: Binary search on the answer with a greedy "how many parts?" check (or DP over split points)

approaches.name: Try every way to place the k − 1 cuts
approaches.idea: Recursively choose where the first part ends, and solve the rest with one part fewer. The cost of a split is its largest part; keep the smallest cost.
steps: `best(i, parts)` = the smallest possible largest sum for `nums[i..]` cut into `parts` pieces.
If `parts == 1`, it is the sum of `nums[i..]`.
Otherwise try every end `j` for the first piece (leaving at least `parts − 1` elements), cost `max(sum(i..j), best(j + 1, parts − 1))`; take the minimum.
approaches.why: There are C(n − 1, k − 1) ways to place the cuts and each is explored separately. Recursion depth is k.

approaches.name: Dynamic programming over (prefix, parts)
approaches.idea: The brute force solves the same subproblems many times. Let `dp[p][i]` = the best largest sum for the first `i` elements in `p` parts; the last part is `nums[j..i − 1]` for some `j`.
steps: Build prefix sums so any part sum is O(1).
`dp[1][i] = prefix[i]`.
For `p` from 2 to k and `i` from p to n: `dp[p][i] = min over j in [p − 1, i − 1] of max(dp[p − 1][j], prefix[i] − prefix[j])`.
Return `dp[k][n]`.
approaches.why: k·n states, each trying up to n split points: 50 × 10⁶ = 5 × 10⁷ steps at most here. Part sums reach 10⁹, so they fit in a 32-bit int, but prefix sums are kept in 64 bits for safety.

approaches.name: Binary search the largest sum
approaches.idea: Turn it around: for a limit `L`, the fewest parts needed (cutting greedily whenever the next value would push the part over `L`) only goes down as `L` grows. Find the smallest `L` that needs at most `k` parts.
steps: Search `L` in `[max(nums), sum(nums)]`.
Count parts greedily for `mid`: start a new part whenever the running sum would exceed `mid`.
If at most `k` parts, `hi = mid`; else `lo = mid + 1`.
Return `lo`. (Needing fewer than `k` parts is fine: a part can always be split further without raising the largest sum.)
approaches.why: S = sum(nums) ≤ 10⁹, so about 30 greedy passes of O(n).
